common_name: How Sweet It Is Corn (AAS-Winning White Sugary-Enhanced Sweet Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 60°F, planting in solid blocks of at least 4 rows for adequate wind pollination; How Sweet It Is, a 1986 All-America Selections winner, is a sugary-enhanced white sweet corn with excellent post-harvest sugar retention.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil in solid blocks rather than single rows to ensure thorough wind pollination of the ears. How Sweet It Is, a 1986 All-America Selections winner, produces pure white, sugary-enhanced kernels with outstanding sweetness and tenderness that hold their sugar content well after harvest rather than quickly converting to starch, giving a longer window of peak eating quality than standard sweet corn. Isolate from field corn, popcorn, or other corn types by at least 250 feet or two weeks of tasseling time to prevent cross-pollination from diluting sweetness. Harvest when ears are well filled and kernels exude a milky liquid when pressed, and cook or refrigerate promptly for the best flavor.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Sweet Corn Variety Evaluation
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Sweet Corn for Florida Gardens

common_name: Merit Corn (Classic Early-Midseason Yellow Hybrid Sweet Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 60°F, planting in solid blocks of at least 4 rows for adequate wind pollination; Merit is a classic early-to-midseason yellow hybrid sweet corn long grown for its reliable, heavy yields.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil in solid blocks rather than single rows to ensure thorough wind pollination of the ears. Merit is a classic standard-sugary yellow hybrid sweet corn that has been a dependable home-garden and market variety for decades, valued for consistent, heavy ear production and good, traditional sweet corn flavor on a vigorous, adaptable plant. Its early-to-midseason maturity makes it a good choice for a first planting in a succession sweet corn schedule through the Gulf South growing season. Harvest when ears are well filled and kernels exude a milky liquid when pressed, and cook or refrigerate promptly, since standard sugary sweet corn converts sugar to starch faster after picking than sugary-enhanced or supersweet types.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Sweet Corn Variety Evaluation
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Sweet Corn for Florida Gardens

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after soil has thoroughly warmed and frost danger has passed; Delicious 51, a classic 1951 USDA commercial release, was a standard cantaloupe variety for decades before modern hybrids became dominant.

directions: Direct sow seed in hills of two to three plants in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once soil has thoroughly warmed. Delicious 51, released by the USDA in 1951, was a standard commercial cantaloupe variety for decades, prized for well-netted rind, thick, sweet, aromatic salmon-orange flesh, and good disease tolerance for its era, and it remains a solid, reliable open-pollinated choice for home gardeners today. The vigorous, sprawling vines need plenty of room to run and benefit from consistent moisture during fruit development, tapering off as fruit nears ripeness to concentrate sugars. Harvest when the melon slips easily from the vine at full slip, with a strong, sweet aroma at the blossom end signaling peak ripeness.

common_name: Rattlesnake Pole Bean (Classic Purple-Streaked Heirloom Pole Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed in warm soil, providing a sturdy pole or trellis; Rattlesnake is a classic heirloom pole snap bean named for the distinctive purple streaking on its green pods.

directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a sturdy pole or trellis for the vigorous climbing vines. Rattlesnake is a classic heirloom pole snap bean named for the purple streaking that mottles its green pods, an old Southern favorite valued for good production even in hot, humid summer conditions that stress many other snap beans, along with reliable flavor and good tolerance of drought once established. The purple markings fade during cooking, leaving a green bean with excellent flavor. Harvest pods young and tender for the best snap bean texture, picking every couple of days to keep the vigorous vines setting new pods through the long growing season.
